intro: Variation X, an Intermezzo marked Allegretto, is Elgar’s portrait of Dora Penny, with a long viola melody set among short, skipping figures and brief pauses. Elgar named her Dorabella after the young woman in Mozart’s Così fan tutte.

sections.label: Var 10 · “Dorabella”, Allegretto, muted violins
sections.mNote: Muted violins play over plucked bass notes.

sections.label: Var 10 · Flute melody over violin figures
sections.mNote: The flute holds long notes above short figures in the violins.

sections.label: Var 10 · Short wind phrases and muted strings
sections.mNote: Short wind phrases alternate with muted strings.

cues.title: Muted violins and pizzicato, rehearsal 38
cues.text: Muted violins enter late in the bar, with short rests between their phrases. The cellos and basses play pizzicato. The broken phrasing alludes to Dora Penny’s slight stammer.
cues.evidence: Novello full score, p. 57, rehearsal 38: muted violins, rests and pizzicato lower strings. The allusion to Penny’s stammer is documented by John Pickard, BBC programme note (2005): https://www.bbc.com/radio3/classical/elgar/notes/note_enigma.shtml
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Dora and her memoir
cues.text: Dora was the daughter of the rector of Wolverhampton and a close friend of the Elgars. Years later, as Mrs Richard Powell, she wrote Edward Elgar: Memories of a Variation.
cues.evidence: Penny’s family and friendship: https://elgar.org/3enigma.htm. Her married name and memoir: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enigma_Variations, variation X.

cues.title: Flute melody over muted violins
cues.text: The flute plays a sustained melody while the muted violins continue their short, broken figures. Earlier in the variation the solo viola has the sustained line.
cues.evidence: Novello full score, pp. 59–60 and 64–65: sustained viola and flute phrases. Elgar singles out these two instruments in his commentary on variation X: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enigma_Variations
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: The flute’s phrase over pizzicato strings
transitions.to: Var 10 · Flute melody over violin figures
transitions.how: The G major dance stays at Allegretto. Over pizzicato cellos and basses, the flute holds its melody across the bar lines. The oboes play short figures between its phrases, and the muted violins continue their off-beat figures.
transitions.evidence: Novello full score, pp. 64–65: sustained flute melody, short oboe figures, muted violins and pizzicato lower strings.

source.title: Elgar, Enigma Variations, full score (Novello)
source.locator: Novello full score, pp. 57–73, rehearsal figures 38–46: muted strings, the solo viola melody and its later flute counterpart.

timeline.note: Muted violins play off the beat above short viola chords and pizzicato low strings (p. 57).
Short wind phrases interrupt the strings’ dance (pp. 57–58).
A solo viola plays a longer melody beneath the short figures in the violins (pp. 59–60).
Bassoons and violas alternate between the short violin phrases (pp. 61–62).
The violins’ skipping figures return, punctuated by quiet wind chords (pp. 63–64).
The flute holds a long melody above the strings’ short, separated notes (pp. 65–66).
Second violins and violas continue the dance while the upper woodwinds rest (pp. 67–68).
Little wind phrases rejoin the violins as the dance nears its end (pp. 69–71).
Winds and muted strings exchange the final phrases over plucked bass notes (pp. 72–73).

composer.epithet: Composer of the Enigma Variations, a set of variations drawn from his friendships, who also recorded his own music for the gramophone.
facts: His father’s Worcester music shop; violin and organ; composition largely self-taught
Powick bandmaster, instrumental teacher and organist at St George’s, Worcester
Two symphonies; violin and cello concertos; Gerontius; five Pomp and Circumstance marches
Master of the King’s Musick from 1924; recordings of his own orchestral works
composer.background:
Elgar grew up among the instruments and sheet music in his father’s Worcester shop. William tuned pianos and played the organ at St George’s Catholic Church; Edward studied the scores, learned several instruments and earned money with his violin. Born at Lower Broadheath on 2 June 1857, he had hoped to study at Leipzig, but the family could not afford it. Playing in the Three Choirs Festival orchestra, he learned the choral music of Handel and Mendelssohn as a member of the string section.

From 1879 to 1884 he was bandmaster at Worcester County Asylum, Powick. He trained members of staff to play for the patients and supplied quadrilles and polkas for the Friday-evening dances. He knew each player in this orchestra individually and had to write within their capabilities. He also taught in local schools and gave private lessons in Malvern. In 1885 he succeeded William at the organ of St George’s.
